title: Design a Developer API Platform with Usage-Based Billing
followUps: Walk through one API request end to end, from the developer's HTTP call to the response, listing every check your gateway makes. What does each one cost in latency, and which ones can be served from memory?
A gateway node crashes after the engine has processed 10,000 requests but before their usage events were durably recorded. How does your design make sure those requests are billed exactly once?
An enterprise partner disputes their invoice, claiming they made 20% fewer calls than you billed. What data do you have to settle the dispute, and how long do you keep it?
A developer's API key is leaked on a public repository and someone starts using it heavily. How is it detected, how is it revoked across every gateway node, and how fast does revocation take effect?
How do you stop the anonymous playground on your marketing site from being used as a free version of the API?

interviewer.approach: Strong answers separate the synchronous request path (auth, quota, rate limit, proxy to the engine) from the asynchronous metering and billing path, and treat billing as a correctness problem rather than a counting problem. Requirements: self-serve sign-up with organizations and members; multiple API keys per org (create, label, rotate, revoke); free, pay-as-you-go and enterprise plans; per-key rate limits and per-org monthly quotas; playground; usage dashboards within minutes; monthly invoices that are exact. Estimates: 2B billable calls/month is ~770/s average, ~20k/s peak; usage events at 20k/s x ~200 bytes = 4 MB/s, ~500 GB/month raw; 50k orgs is tiny metadata. Request path: TLS terminates at a regional gateway; API key is a random secret with a public prefix (for display/lookups) and is stored only as a hash; the gateway caches key -> org/plan/limits in memory with a short TTL plus push invalidation for revocations (pub/sub), so auth costs no network hop. Rate limits per key with a token bucket in Redis (Lua script) or local buckets with a global budget split across nodes; monthly quota checked against an approximate running counter (soft limit, with overage policy per plan) rather than the exact billing ledger. Errors: 401/403/429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers; request ids on every response. Metering: the gateway emits a usage event per request with a unique request id (and the units: characters or suggestion count) to a durable log (Kafka) asynchronously, buffered locally with a write-ahead file so a crash doesn't lose events; consumers deduplicate on request id (idempotent upsert) and aggregate into per-org/per-key per-minute rollups (stream processor) for dashboards; raw events kept in object storage for audits. Billing: at period close, a batch job computes usage per org from the deduplicated store, applies the plan's pricing (tiers, included units, overage, committed spend for enterprise), writes immutable invoice line items, and hands invoices to the payment provider with an idempotency key; late events after close go into the next invoice as adjustments. Playground: runs through the same gateway with a special low-quota key per signed-in user, or anonymous with CAPTCHA, strict per-IP limits, short input caps, and no raw API responses beyond what the UI needs. Multi-region: keys and plans replicated globally; usage written regionally and aggregated centrally. Observability: per-org latency/error dashboards, alerts for partner SLAs.
hints: Which work has to happen before you can answer the request, and which can happen after? Where does billing belong?
How would the gateway check an API key on every request without a database round trip, and still honour a revocation quickly?
If the same usage event is delivered twice, or a gateway dies before sending it, what happens to the bill? What would make counting idempotent?
Is the counter you use to enforce quotas the same one you should bill from? What accuracy does each need?
The playground is on a public page. Whose credentials does it use, and what limits apply?
pitfalls: Writing a row to the primary database (or incrementing a SQL counter) synchronously on every API call, which adds latency and becomes the bottleneck at peak.
Storing API keys in plaintext, or looking them up in the database on every request without caching.
Billing from the rate limiter's counters, which are approximate, reset, and not auditable.
Fire-and-forget usage events with no deduplication or durability, so crashes lose revenue and retries double-bill.
Treating quotas and rate limits as the same thing: per-second burst protection versus monthly plan entitlements.
Ignoring late-arriving events and period boundaries when closing an invoice.
No story for key revocation propagation, or one that relies on cache expiry of many minutes.
Exposing an unlimited playground backed by a shared internal key.
facts: About 50,000 developer organizations, from hobbyists to about 300 enterprise partners. Each org has members and up to 50 API keys.
Plans: Free (10,000 calls per month), Pay-as-you-go (per-call pricing with volume tiers), and Enterprise (committed annual spend, custom limits, 99.9% monthly uptime SLA).
Traffic is about 2 billion billable calls per month; peak is about 20,000 calls per second, dominated by a few large partners.
The engine takes 50 to 300 ms per call. The platform may add at most 20 ms at p99 on top of the engine.
A call's billable units depend on the input size (per 1,000 characters), which the gateway knows when the request arrives.
Usage dashboards should be accurate to within about 5 minutes. Invoices must be exact: no call billed twice and no billable call missed.
Free-plan keys are hard-limited; paid plans continue past their included amount and are billed overage. Every key also has a per-second rate limit (default 50 requests per second).
Developers can create, label, rotate and revoke keys in the developer hub. A revoked key must stop working everywhere within 1 minute.
The developer hub has an interactive playground on public documentation pages; signed-in developers can try requests without creating a key.
The API is served from two regions (US and EU); EU customers require their text to be processed in the EU.
Raw usage records must be kept for 13 months to resolve billing disputes.
deepDives: Gateway request path: API key hashing and lookup, in-memory caching, and fast revocation
Rate limits versus monthly quotas: where each is enforced and how accurate each must be
Exactly-once usage metering: request ids, durable local buffering, a log, and idempotent aggregation
From usage to invoice: period close, pricing tiers, late events, and idempotent handoff to the payment provider
Protecting the playground and free tier from abuse
